prod_012:n6.computerUseWhy: An agent can draft resubmission notes and update store metadata, but a human must judge how to address the specific rejection reason and confirm compliance.

growth_014:n2.why: Choosing which existing customers keep old pricing is a strategic tradeoff between revenue capture and churn risk that only leadership can weigh.
growth_014:n2.computerUseWhy: This is a judgment call about business risk tolerance and customer relationships, not a task performed through any interface.

hr_010:n1.why: Setting the scorecard and comp band requires a live negotiation and alignment with the board on strategic priorities and budget.
hr_010:n1.computerUseWhy: This is an interpersonal deliberation with the board, not a form-based or system-driven task.

hr_010:n2.why: Selecting and engaging a retained executive search firm involves negotiating scope, fee structure, and fit with a human vendor relationship.
hr_010:n2.computerUseWhy: This requires relationship-based vendor negotiation, not something an agent can execute through a screen.

hr_010:n2b.why: Signing the search engagement letter creates a binding financial and contractual obligation that must carry an authorized officer's signature.
hr_010:n2b.computerUseWhy: Even though e-signature tools exist, the signature itself carries legal authority that only an authorized human officer can grant.

hr_010:n4.why: Interviewing candidates and checking references requires live conversation and subjective evaluation of fit and character.
hr_010:n4.computerUseWhy: These are in-person or live interpersonal interactions that no interface can substitute for.

hr_010:n6.why: Executive compensation and equity grants require formal board approval under corporate governance and securities law obligations.
hr_010:n6.computerUseWhy: Approving and signing the grant consent is a board governance act with legal weight that cannot be delegated to an agent.

hr_010:n8.why: The step depends on the candidate's personal decision to accept the offer, which is outside company control.
hr_010:n8.computerUseWhy: There is no interface to operate; the process is paused until the candidate independently decides to accept.

hr_011:n1.why: Choosing between H-1B, O-1, or TN requires immigration counsel's legal judgment about the candidate's qualifications and the strategy most likely to succeed under USCIS rules.
hr_011:n1.computerUseWhy: This is a legal consultation and strategic judgment call between counsel and the employer, not a form or portal interaction.

hr_011:n3.why: The Labor Condition Application requires the employer's authorized signatory to attest under penalty of perjury to wage and working-condition compliance before DOL will accept it.
hr_011:n3.computerUseWhy: An agent can fill and stage the FLAG.dol.gov LCA form, but the final attestation/submission must be executed by the authorized company signatory.

hr_011:n4.why: DOL's statutory 7-business-day LCA certification window is a fixed government processing timeline outside the employer's control.
hr_011:n4.computerUseWhy: There is no action to take; the employer is simply waiting on DOL's internal adjudication clock.

hr_011:n5.why: I-129 requires the petitioning employer's signature attesting under penalty of perjury to the accuracy of the visa petition, a legal responsibility that cannot be delegated.
hr_011:n5.computerUseWhy: Signing carries personal legal liability for the petitioner, so an agent cannot substitute even though the physical act of signing is trivial.

hr_011:n6.why: USCIS requires the signed I-129 package and fee submission to come from an authorized filer taking legal responsibility for its accuracy.
hr_011:n6.computerUseWhy: An agent can populate and upload documents in the USCIS online filing portal, but the authorized signer must complete and confirm submission.

hr_011:n7.why: USCIS adjudication time depends entirely on the agency's internal caseload and processing queue.
hr_011:n7.computerUseWhy: Nothing to operate; the employer is waiting on USCIS's own review timeline.

hr_012:n1.why: Selecting a 401(k) provider involves comparing fee structures, fund menus, and service quality that require a business judgment call by the founder or HR lead.
hr_012:n1.computerUseWhy: An agent can research and tabulate provider options (e.g., Guideline, Human Interest) but the final vendor choice is a human decision.

hr_012:n2.why: Setting the employer match and eligibility rules is a compensation-policy decision tied to budget and retention strategy that only company leadership can make.
hr_012:n2.computerUseWhy: An agent can model match-cost scenarios and eligibility tiers, but leadership must decide the final match formula.

hr_012:n3.why: Adopting a 401(k) plan document is a fiduciary act under ERISA requiring an authorized officer's binding signature.
hr_012:n3.computerUseWhy: The e-signature step carries ERISA fiduciary and legal liability, so it must be executed by an authorized officer, not an agent.

hr_013:n1.why: Choosing an Employer of Record and comparing country employment costs requires judgment about total cost, compliance risk, and service coverage per country.
hr_013:n1.computerUseWhy: An agent can pull and compare EOR pricing/quotes (e.g., Deel, Remote) across countries, but the final vendor selection is a human call.

hr_013:n3.why: The employment agreement must be signed by the candidate themselves through the EOR's own onboarding flow, an action outside the company's control.
hr_013:n3.computerUseWhy: The company is waiting on the candidate's independent act of signing via the EOR platform, not operating any screen itself.

hr_013:n4.why: Right-to-work and background checks are run and completed by Deel's third-party verification process on its own timeline.
hr_013:n4.computerUseWhy: The step is purely waiting on Deel's vendor-run background check pipeline to return results.

hr_013:n5.why: Deel's EOR platform requires selecting country-specific payroll/benefits plans and equipment logistics that are pre-configured administrative choices, not legal judgment calls.
hr_013:n5.computerUseWhy: An agent can log into the Deel portal and complete the payroll/benefits/equipment setup forms using pre-decided plan selections.

ops_013:n1.why: Choosing an MDM vendor is a budget and security-posture tradeoff that only the ops/IT owner can commit to.
ops_013:n1.computerUseWhy: An agent can research and compare MDM vendors (Jamf, Kandji, Intune) and produce a recommendation, but a human must make the final selection.

ops_013:n2.why: Apple requires a verified company representative to attest legal authority over the organization (often via phone/D-U-N-S verification) before granting Business Manager access.
ops_013:n2.computerUseWhy: The enrollment form is trivial to fill but Apple's identity/authority verification of the enrolling representative blocks an agent from completing it unsupervised.

ops_013:n4.why: Physically unboxing, imaging, and handing out laptops to distributed employees is hands-on fleet logistics work.
ops_013:n4.computerUseWhy: Enrolling physical devices requires in-person handling and shipping of hardware, not a screen to drive.

ops_014:n1.why: Sizing headcount and budget for office space depends on internal growth forecasts and financial constraints only leadership can judge.
ops_014:n1.computerUseWhy: This is an internal planning decision made through discussion and judgment, not an interface an agent can operate.

ops_014:n2.why: Touring candidate office spaces requires physically walking the property with a broker to assess condition and fit.
ops_014:n2.computerUseWhy: Site visits are in-person physical inspections with no digital interface to drive.

ops_014:n4.why: LOI terms (rent, TI allowance, term, exit rights) are settled through back-and-forth negotiation with the landlord's broker requiring commercial judgment and leverage.
ops_014:n4.computerUseWhy: Negotiation is an interpersonal exchange of offers and counteroffers, not a form-driven process an agent can execute.

ops_014:n5.why: Only an attorney can assess and accept the legal risk embedded in a commercial lease's indemnities, guarantees, and default clauses.
ops_014:n5.computerUseWhy: Reading the lease document is trivial but the substantive legal risk sign-off must come from counsel, not an agent.

ops_014:n6.why: Signing the lease and personal/corporate guarantee creates binding legal and financial liability that only an authorized officer can accept.
ops_014:n6.computerUseWhy: Clicking through an e-sign flow is mechanically trivial, but the officer's legal authority to bind the company to the guarantee is the actual gate.

ops_014:n8.why: Landlords require a standard certificate of insurance naming them as additional insured, which Embroker issues through a self-service request form.
ops_014:n8.computerUseWhy: An agent can log into the Embroker portal and generate/send the COI using existing policy data.

ops_014:n9.why: Setting up internet, utility, and access accounts is a series of standard ISP/utility provider sign-up forms tied to the new address.
ops_014:n9.computerUseWhy: An agent can complete the ISP and utility provider web forms with the company's account and address details.

comp_014:n1.why: Deciding how to prioritize a questionnaire depends on the deal's revenue size and deadline pressure, a judgment call for the deal/security owner.
comp_014:n1.computerUseWhy: An agent can scan the questionnaire and flag size/deadline/risk signals, but a human must decide the triage priority and resourcing.

comp_014:n4.why: A security lead must judge whether draft answers accurately represent the company's actual controls before they become a contractual representation to the customer.
comp_014:n4.computerUseWhy: Approving risk-laden security disclosures carries legal and contractual liability that requires a human security authority, not just form-filling.

comp_014:n5.why: The customer's vendor-risk portal requires the finalized questionnaire to be uploaded and submitted through their specific web form.
comp_014:n5.computerUseWhy: A browser agent can log into the customer's portal, fill in the approved answers, and click submit since it's a deterministic web flow with no approval gate.

sw_010:n7.why: Engineers must debate and agree on which repo actions and permissions are safe to expose to an autonomous coding agent before granting access.
sw_010:n7.computerUseWhy: This is a team discussion/decision-making meeting about policy, not an action performed on any single screen or portal.

growth_015:n4.why: A budget owner must authorize the marketing spend on discount offers before the win-back sequence goes out.
growth_015:n4.computerUseWhy: Approving a discount budget commits real company funds and requires the financial authority of a manager, even though clicking approve is trivial.

opp_001:n3.why: Releasing a wire/ACH payment is the final financial-control checkpoint required by the bank's dual-control policy to prevent unauthorized fund movement.
opp_001:n3.computerUseWhy: Clicking 'release' in the banking dashboard is trivial, but the release action itself is the fraud-control authorization point and must be exercised by an accountable human, not an agent.

opp_002:n2.why: Only the contractor holds their own SSN/EIN and bank routing details, which they must self-report on the W-9 and payroll form.
opp_002:n2.computerUseWhy: This is the contractor's own action on an external party's timeline; there is no internal screen for the company's agent to drive.

opp_007:n4.why: MFA enrollment binds the account to the new hire's personal device and identity per the org's security policy, so it cannot be completed by anyone other than that employee.
opp_007:n4.computerUseWhy: The sign-in and MFA screens exist, but security policy requires the actual employee to authenticate with their own device/phone, blocking delegation to an agent.

opp_012:n2.why: Selecting a trademark watch vendor or outside counsel is a legal-risk-tolerance and cost decision tied to the brand's IP strategy.
opp_012:n2.computerUseWhy: An agent can research and compare watch services (e.g., Corsearch, Trademarkia) and summarize pricing/coverage, but a human must choose the vendor or engage counsel.

brand_003:n2.why: Choosing the brand palette direction is a subjective creative/aesthetic decision tied to brand identity that only a founder or designer can validate.
brand_003:n2.computerUseWhy: An agent can generate and present palette options (e.g., via Coolors or design research), but the human must make the final aesthetic selection.

team_001:n2.why: Only the invited teammate can accept the invite email and set their own account credentials.
team_001:n2.computerUseWhy: This step is entirely the external invitee's action on their own timeline; there is no internal screen for the company to operate.

vendor_010:n2.why: Granting OAuth access or issuing an API key requires the vendor account owner's authenticated consent to permit data sharing with the integration.
vendor_010:n2.computerUseWhy: An agent can navigate the vendor's OAuth consent screen or API key generation page, but the account owner must log in and click 'Allow' to authorize the credential grant.
